brief_actual_contribution: Introduces AIP, a black-box attack that crafts natural-looking adversarial instructional prompts (paired with poisoned documents and a stealthy trigger) to covertly steer RAG retrieval and generation toward attacker-targeted outputs while preserving clean-task utility.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Indirect prompt injection differs from factual poisoning. Instead of inserting false evidence, the attacker inserts instructions that are retrieved and interpreted by the LLM as commands. In practice, an indirect prompt injection must overcome the retrieval barrier: the malicious document must actually be retrieved under natural queries. \citet{rrag005} explicitly study this barrier and propose trigger fragments that improve retrieval of attack fragments. AIP broadens the surface further by showing that shared instructional prompts can be weaponized to steer RAG retrieval and generation \citep{aip2025}. These attacks imply that prompt templates, document ingestion rules, and retrieved text should be treated as untrusted inputs.

This intervention map helps explain why papers sometimes appear to solve the same problem while actually operating at different layers. For example, irrelevant-context filtering \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, Chain-of-Note \citep{chainOfNote2023}, and Sufficient Context \citep{sufficientContext2024} all address unreliable evidence, but the first filters evidence, the second changes generator reasoning, and the third changes answer policy. Similarly, PoisonedRAG-style attacks \citep{poisonedRAG2024} target the corpus-to-generation path, while AIP attacks prompt templates \citep{aip2025}. A comprehensive survey must therefore compare methods by intervention point, not only by reported task accuracy.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: \paragraph{Evidence reliability dimensions.} We use \emph{evidence reliability} as an umbrella concept with six dimensions. \textbf{Relevance} asks whether the evidence is about the query. \textbf{Sufficiency} asks whether it contains enough information to answer. \textbf{Faithfulness support} asks whether the final claim is entailed by the evidence rather than merely related. \textbf{Consistency} asks whether different evidence sources agree. \textbf{Provenance and freshness} ask where the evidence came from and whether it is up to date. \textbf{Integrity} asks whether the evidence has been manipulated. Existing work usually studies one or two of these dimensions at a time. For example, irrelevant-context robustness focuses on relevance and distraction \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, sufficient-context work focuses on answerability \citep{sufficientContext2024}, conflict work focuses on consistency \citep{tugOfWar2024,faithfulRAG2025}, and poisoning work focuses on integrity \citep{poisonedRAG2024,badRAG2024}. A central goal of this survey is to place these dimensions in one framework.

Corpus poisoning attacks insert malicious passages into the retrieval database so that they are returned for target queries. Early work on poisoning retrieval corpora demonstrates that small numbers of adversarial passages can manipulate dense retrieval \citep{poisoningRetrievalCorpora2023}. PoisonedRAG extends this threat to end-to-end generation: retrieved malicious passages can cause the LLM to output attacker-chosen answers \citep{poisonedRAG2024}. BadRAG, UniC-RAG, and related methods explore different trigger structures, optimization objectives, and attack settings \citep{badRAG2024,rrag049,rrag057}. The important lesson is that retrieval augmentation can amplify small corpus changes into large generation effects.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Calibration asks whether confidence matches correctness. In RAG, confidence depends on both model uncertainty and evidence uncertainty. contexts_supplied.paragraph: Defenses against adversarial corruption operate at multiple layers. Certified approaches such as RobustRAG isolate and aggregate outputs to provide guarantees under bounded retrieval corruption \citep{certifiedRAG2024}. Reranking defenses such as ProGRank use instability or probe-gradient signals to demote suspicious passages \citep{rrag004}. Traceback methods attempt to identify poisoned texts after an attack has occurred \citep{rrag128}.

Robustness therefore depends on both retriever quality and generator selectivity.

brief_actual_contribution: Introduces the original Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework combining a DPR retriever with a BART generator, fine-tuned end-to-end for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a parametric language model with non-parametric evidence retrieved at inference time \citep{lewis2020rag}. The paradigm has become central to open-domain question answering, enterprise assistants, scientific search, medical and legal support, and agentic systems. RAG promises to reduce hallucination, update knowledge without retraining, and produce source-grounded answers. However, as RAG moves from curated benchmarks to open, mutable, and adversarial environments, the retrieved evidence becomes a first-order source of risk.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: Phantom proposes injecting a single malicious document into a RAG knowledge base to mount a backdoor poisoning attack triggered by a natural token sequence in user queries, without modifying the generator.
Two-stage optimization to craft poisoned document that induces refusal, biased opinions, harmful outputs, exfiltration; demonstrated on multiple LLMs and ChatRTX.

brief_actual_contribution: Phantom is a backdoor poisoning attack on RAG that uses a two-stage optimization (HotFlip on retriever + Multi-Coordinate Gradient on generator) to craft a single poisoned document retrieved only when a natural trigger appears in the query, enabling refusal, biased opinion, harmful behavior, passage exfiltration, and tool misuse across open and closed LLMs including a black-box attack on NVIDIA ChatRTX.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Backdoor-style attacks make the threat more persistent. TrojanRAG and Phantom show that triggers can activate malicious behavior through retrieved contexts without changing the generator weights \citep{trojanRAG2024,phantom2024}. contexts_supplied.paragraph: \paragraph{Evidence reliability dimensions.} We use \emph{evidence reliability} as an umbrella concept with six dimensions. \textbf{Relevance} asks whether the evidence is about the query. \textbf{Sufficiency} asks whether it contains enough information to answer. \textbf{Faithfulness support} asks whether the final claim is entailed by the evidence rather than merely related. \textbf{Consistency} asks whether different evidence sources agree. \textbf{Provenance and freshness} ask where the evidence came from and whether it is up to date. \textbf{Integrity} asks whether the evidence has been manipulated. Existing work usually studies one or two of these dimensions at a time. For example, irrelevant-context robustness focuses on relevance and distraction \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, sufficient-context work focuses on answerability \citep{sufficientContext2024}, conflict work focuses on consistency \citep{tugOfWar2024,faithfulRAG2025}, and poisoning work focuses on integrity \citep{poisonedRAG2024,badRAG2024}. A central goal of this survey is to place these dimensions in one framework.

Corpus poisoning attacks insert malicious passages into the retrieval database so that they are returned for target queries. Early work on poisoning retrieval corpora demonstrates that small numbers of adversarial passages can manipulate dense retrieval \citep{poisoningRetrievalCorpora2023}. PoisonedRAG extends this threat to end-to-end generation: retrieved malicious passages can cause the LLM to output attacker-chosen answers \citep{poisonedRAG2024}. BadRAG, UniC-RAG, and related methods explore different trigger structures, optimization objectives, and attack settings \citep{badRAG2024,rrag049,rrag057}. The important lesson is that retrieval augmentation can amplify small corpus changes into large generation effects.

This intervention map helps explain why papers sometimes appear to solve the same problem while actually operating at different layers. For example, irrelevant-context filtering \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, Chain-of-Note \citep{chainOfNote2023}, and Sufficient Context \citep{sufficientContext2024} all address unreliable evidence, but the first filters evidence, the second changes generator reasoning, and the third changes answer policy. Similarly, PoisonedRAG-style attacks \citep{poisonedRAG2024} target the corpus-to-generation path, while AIP attacks prompt templates \citep{aip2025}. A comprehensive survey must therefore compare methods by intervention point, not only by reported task accuracy.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Evidence noise does not begin at retrieval scoring. Query formulation is itself a brittle interface. Query-level robustness work shows that minor changes in wording can substantially affect retrieval and downstream answers \citep{queryRobustness2025}. This suggests that robust RAG should include query normalization, query expansion, and query uncertainty estimation. In multi-turn settings, the query may be non-standalone or under-specified, making retrieval quality depend on dialogue state tracking \citep{rrag141}. The retriever may also inherit biases from chunking and indexing: relevant facts can be split across chunks, qualifiers can be separated from claims, and embeddings can overemphasize topical similarity over answer sufficiency.

We group robust RAG evaluation into six families: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Noise robustness}: performance as irrelevant or misleading passages are injected, removed, reordered, or ranked higher. \item \textbf{Distraction sensitivity}: whether answer or confidence changes when distractors are added while gold evidence remains available. \item \textbf{Conflict sensitivity}: whether the system detects and resolves parametric--retrieved or retrieved--retrieved contradictions. \item \textbf{Adversarial robustness}: attack success rate, poisoned retrieval rate, trigger robustness, defense bypass rate, and recovery after filtering. \item \textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction}: selective risk, abstention precision/recall, expected calibration error, and clarification quality. \item \textbf{End-to-end action quality}: whether the system chooses the right policy among answer, retrieve, re-retrieve, filter, abstain, or ask. \end{enumerate} Benchmarking work such as RGB, RAGTruth, robustness-at-query-level analyses, poisoning benchmarks, and uncertainty benchmarks provides pieces of this landscape \citep{rgb2023,ragTruth2024,queryRobustness2025}. brief_actual_contribution: Categorizes retrieval noise into relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual types, proposes RAAT (adaptive adversarial training with noise-aware multi-task learning), and introduces RAG-Bench for evaluating noise robustness on three open-domain QA datasets.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Subsequent work expands the typology of noise. \citet{raat2024} distinguishes multiple retrieval-noise types and trains models with adaptive adversarial objectives and explicit noise awareness. The distinction matters: an irrelevant passage that is obviously off-topic may be easy to ignore, while a counterfactual or hard-negative passage may be semantically close to the query and therefore much more dangerous. RGB similarly evaluates noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness as separate abilities \citep{rgb2023}. Taken together, these works suggest that ``RAG robustness'' cannot be measured by a single noisy-context accuracy number. A strong evaluation should vary the type, quantity, ranking position, and semantic hardness of negative evidence.

Training-based approaches expose the generator to noise so that it learns to separate relevant from irrelevant context \citep{raat2024,rrag091}. This can improve robustness but also raises a scalability question: robust training may be less effective or less necessary as base LLMs become stronger, and adversarially generated noise can overfit to a particular retriever or generator. Training-free approaches, such as filtering and note-taking, are easier to add to existing systems but depend on reliable relevance or sufficiency signals. A recurring pattern is that no single pre-generation control is sufficient: retrieval filtering reduces easy noise, reranking handles ordering, compression improves context budget, and downstream calibration remains necessary for residual uncertainty.

brief_actual_contribution: Introduces URAG, a benchmark that reformulates open-ended RAG tasks into MCQA and applies conformal prediction to jointly evaluate accuracy and uncertainty of 8 RAG methods across 5 domains, including under irrelevant/noisy retrieval.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Recent benchmarks make this point more explicit. Magic Mushroom introduces fine-grained retrieval noise categories, including distracting and low-quality evidence \citep{rrag027}. URAG formulates uncertainty quantification in RAG and studies the effect of irrelevant and noisy retrieval on conformal prediction \citep{rrag001}. PRGB and other placeholder or perturbation-based benchmarks test whether models remain robust when retrieval context is systematically manipulated \citep{rrag183}. The trajectory of this literature is clear: robust RAG evaluation is moving from ``add random distractors'' to controlled stress tests that expose distinct failure mechanisms.

We group robust RAG evaluation into six families: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Noise robustness}: performance as irrelevant or misleading passages are injected, removed, reordered, or ranked higher. \item \textbf{Distraction sensitivity}: whether answer or confidence changes when distractors are added while gold evidence remains available. \item \textbf{Conflict sensitivity}: whether the system detects and resolves parametric--retrieved or retrieved--retrieved contradictions. \item \textbf{Adversarial robustness}: attack success rate, poisoned retrieval rate, trigger robustness, defense bypass rate, and recovery after filtering. \item \textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction}: selective risk, abstention precision/recall, expected calibration error, and clarification quality. \item \textbf{End-to-end action quality}: whether the system chooses the right policy among answer, retrieve, re-retrieve, filter, abstain, or ask. \end{enumerate} Benchmarking work such as RGB, RAGTruth, robustness-at-query-level analyses, poisoning benchmarks, and uncertainty benchmarks provides pieces of this landscape \citep{rgb2023,ragTruth2024,queryRobustness2025}. RGB is useful because it separates RAG abilities rather than reporting one score \citep{rgb2023}. RAGTruth contributes fine-grained hallucination annotations that support detection and attribution \citep{ragTruth2024}. Query-level robustness work shows that the query--retrieval interface is itself fragile \citep{queryRobustness2025}. PoisonArena-style benchmarks and LIAR-style attack evaluations stress adversarial settings rather than benign retrieval noise \citep{rrag023,rrag035}. URAG and uncertainty benchmarks evaluate whether systems know when their answers are reliable \citep{rrag001,rrag093}.

brief_actual_contribution: Identifies a nonlinear 'first drop of ink' effect where a small fraction of hard distractors in long contexts disproportionately degrades QA accuracy, with theoretical analysis via attention/softmax mechanics and validation on retrieval heads.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Distraction is stronger than irrelevance. A passage is distracting when it has negative marginal utility: adding it changes the answer, confidence, attribution, or reasoning path in a harmful direction. This explains why more retrieval is not always better. In long-context settings, retrieving more passages can increase the chance that a hard negative appears before or near useful evidence. \citet{rrag039} study long-context RAG and show why ordering and hard negatives become central once the generator can consume many passages. \citet{rrag003} identify a nonlinear ``first drop of ink'' effect: a small amount of misleading information can disproportionately degrade reasoning. CUB evaluates context-utilization techniques across gold, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts \citep{rrag032}, while UDCG redefines retrieval evaluation around downstream utility rather than traditional relevance alone \citep{rrag058}.

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes ProGRank, a training-free retriever-side reranking defense that uses probe-gradient instability signals under randomized perturbations to demote poisoned passages in dense-retriever RAG.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Defenses against adversarial corruption operate at multiple layers. Certified approaches such as RobustRAG isolate and aggregate outputs to provide guarantees under bounded retrieval corruption \citep{certifiedRAG2024}. Reranking defenses such as ProGRank use instability or probe-gradient signals to demote suspicious passages \citep{rrag004}. Attention-based filters detect abnormal attention patterns caused by poisoned evidence \citep{rrag015}. Clustering and conflict-resolution defenses such as TrustRAG and SeCon-RAG filter semantically inconsistent or suspicious evidence before generation \citep{rrag013,rrag017}. Traceback methods attempt to identify poisoned texts after an attack has occurred \citep{rrag128}.

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes a black-box CEM-based prefix optimization to guarantee retrieval of injected malicious documents (trigger fragment + attack fragment), enabling end-to-end indirect prompt injection attacks against RAG and agentic systems, evaluated across 11 BEIR benchmarks and 8 embedding models.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Indirect prompt injection differs from factual poisoning. Instead of inserting false evidence, the attacker inserts instructions that are retrieved and interpreted by the LLM as commands. In practice, an indirect prompt injection must overcome the retrieval barrier: the malicious document must actually be retrieved under natural queries. \citet{rrag005} explicitly study this barrier and propose trigger fragments that improve retrieval of attack fragments. AIP broadens the surface further by showing that shared instructional prompts can be weaponized to steer RAG retrieval and generation \citep{aip2025}. These attacks imply that prompt templates, document ingestion rules, and retrieved text should be treated as untrusted inputs.

Attack success rate is necessary but insufficient. A strong RAG attack must also be stealthy, durable, and retrieval-realistic. Stealth means poisoned passages should not be trivially detected by lexical filters or human inspection. Durability means attacks should persist under chunking, reranking, context filtering, and prompt changes. Retrieval realism means the malicious content must be retrieved under natural user queries, not only under attacker-crafted queries. Work on indirect prompt injection in the wild explicitly highlights this retrieval barrier \citep{rrag005}. Recent stealth and attention-aware work similarly argues that defenses should evaluate whether poisoned content can be distinguished from benign evidence \citep{rrag015}.

brief_actual_contribution: Defines and systematically evaluates over-searching in search-augmented LLMs, introduces the Tokens Per Correctness (TPC) metric, and releases the OverSearchQA benchmark for abstention/efficiency evaluation.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Recent work also shows that retrieval can be over-used. Over-searching studies introduce metrics such as tokens-per-correctness and benchmarks that measure when search-augmented systems retrieve unnecessarily \citep{rrag006}. Adaptive retrieval without self-knowledge benchmarks many uncertainty-estimation methods and shows that retrieval policies must be evaluated for both accuracy and efficiency \citep{rrag034}. The emerging view is that retrieval is a budgeted decision: each retrieval step trades cost, latency, exposure to noise, and potential accuracy gain.

Control policies are constrained by cost and latency. Multi-query retrieval, reranking, entailment verification, and self-consistency can improve reliability but increase token cost and response time. Over-searching work makes this explicit by measuring the cost of unnecessary search \citep{rrag006}. In enterprise settings, retrieval may also be constrained by access control, privacy, and logging requirements. A useful research direction is risk-adaptive computation: cheap pipelines for low-risk queries, stronger verification for high-risk domains, and human review for cases with high uncertainty or high potential harm.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Conflict-aware methods differ in granularity. FaithfulRAG extracts parametric self-facts, aligns them with retrieved facts, localizes discrepancies, and uses a self-thinking step before generation \citep{faithfulRAG2025}. Astute RAG elicits internal knowledge and consolidates it with retrieved passages through source-aware reliability comparison \citep{astuteRAG2025}. These methods share a principle: conflict should be represented explicitly before the final answer is produced.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Defenses against adversarial corruption operate at multiple layers. Certified approaches such as RobustRAG isolate and aggregate outputs to provide guarantees under bounded retrieval corruption \citep{certifiedRAG2024}. Reranking defenses such as ProGRank use instability or probe-gradient signals to demote suspicious passages \citep{rrag004}. Attention-based filters detect abnormal attention patterns caused by poisoned evidence \citep{rrag015}. Clustering and conflict-resolution defenses such as TrustRAG and SeCon-RAG filter semantically inconsistent or suspicious evidence before generation \citep{rrag013,rrag017}. Attack success rate is necessary but insufficient. A strong RAG attack must also be stealthy, durable, and retrieval-realistic. Stealth means poisoned passages should not be trivially detected by lexical filters or human inspection. Durability means attacks should persist under chunking, reranking, context filtering, and prompt changes. Retrieval realism means the malicious content must be retrieved under natural user queries, not only under attacker-crafted queries. Work on indirect prompt injection in the wild explicitly highlights this retrieval barrier \citep{rrag005}. Recent stealth and attention-aware work similarly argues that defenses should evaluate whether poisoned content can be distinguished from benign evidence \citep{rrag015}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: We group robust RAG evaluation into six families: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Noise robustness}: performance as irrelevant or misleading passages are injected, removed, reordered, or ranked higher. \item \textbf{Distraction sensitivity}: whether answer or confidence changes when distractors are added while gold evidence remains available. \item \textbf{Conflict sensitivity}: whether the system detects and resolves parametric--retrieved or retrieved--retrieved contradictions. \item \textbf{Adversarial robustness}: attack success rate, poisoned retrieval rate, trigger robustness, defense bypass rate, and recovery after filtering. \item \textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction}: selective risk, abstention precision/recall, expected calibration error, and clarification quality. \item \textbf{End-to-end action quality}: whether the system chooses the right policy among answer, retrieve, re-retrieve, filter, abstain, or ask. \end{enumerate} Benchmarking work such as RGB, RAGTruth, robustness-at-query-level analyses, poisoning benchmarks, and uncertainty benchmarks provides pieces of this landscape \citep{rgb2023,ragTruth2024,queryRobustness2025}. RGB is useful because it separates RAG abilities rather than reporting one score \citep{rgb2023}. RAGTruth contributes fine-grained hallucination annotations that support detection and attribution \citep{ragTruth2024}. Query-level robustness work shows that the query--retrieval interface is itself fragile \citep{queryRobustness2025}. brief_actual_contribution: CUB benchmarks seven context-utilisation manipulation techniques across 11 LMs on CounterFact, NQ, and DRUID under gold, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts, revealing trade-offs between faithfulness and robustness.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Distraction is stronger than irrelevance. A passage is distracting when it has negative marginal utility: adding it changes the answer, confidence, attribution, or reasoning path in a harmful direction. This explains why more retrieval is not always better. In long-context settings, retrieving more passages can increase the chance that a hard negative appears before or near useful evidence. \citet{rrag039} study long-context RAG and show why ordering and hard negatives become central once the generator can consume many passages. \citet{rrag003} identify a nonlinear ``first drop of ink'' effect: a small amount of misleading information can disproportionately degrade reasoning. CUB evaluates context-utilization techniques across gold, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts \citep{rrag032}, while UDCG redefines retrieval evaluation around downstream utility rather than traditional relevance alone \citep{rrag058}.

Other approaches manipulate the context itself. Context compression and filtering reduce the amount of irrelevant information passed to the model, while context-utilization benchmarks test whether models actually rely on gold evidence when it is present and ignore conflicting or irrelevant evidence when it is not \citep{rrag032}. The key distinction is between \emph{context availability} and \emph{context use}. A passage can be present in the prompt but ignored; a misleading passage can be unsupported but still dominate the answer. Thus, robust RAG must evaluate how models allocate attention, probability mass, and rationales across sources.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: We group robust RAG evaluation into six families: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Noise robustness}: performance as irrelevant or misleading passages are injected, removed, reordered, or ranked higher. \item \textbf{Distraction sensitivity}: whether answer or confidence changes when distractors are added while gold evidence remains available. \item \textbf{Conflict sensitivity}: whether the system detects and resolves parametric--retrieved or retrieved--retrieved contradictions. \item \textbf{Adversarial robustness}: attack success rate, poisoned retrieval rate, trigger robustness, defense bypass rate, and recovery after filtering. \item \textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction}: selective risk, abstention precision/recall, expected calibration error, and clarification quality. \item \textbf{End-to-end action quality}: whether the system chooses the right policy among answer, retrieve, re-retrieve, filter, abstain, or ask. \end{enumerate} Benchmarking work such as RGB, RAGTruth, robustness-at-query-level analyses, poisoning benchmarks, and uncertainty benchmarks provides pieces of this landscape \citep{rgb2023,ragTruth2024,queryRobustness2025}. RGB is useful because it separates RAG abilities rather than reporting one score \citep{rgb2023}. RAGTruth contributes fine-grained hallucination annotations that support detection and attribution \citep{ragTruth2024}. Query-level robustness work shows that the query--retrieval interface is itself fragile \citep{queryRobustness2025}. PoisonArena-style benchmarks and LIAR-style attack evaluations stress adversarial settings rather than benign retrieval noise \citep{rrag023,rrag035}. contexts_supplied.paragraph: Distraction is stronger than irrelevance. A passage is distracting when it has negative marginal utility: adding it changes the answer, confidence, attribution, or reasoning path in a harmful direction. This explains why more retrieval is not always better. In long-context settings, retrieving more passages can increase the chance that a hard negative appears before or near useful evidence. \citet{rrag039} study long-context RAG and show why ordering and hard negatives become central once the generator can consume many passages. \citet{rrag003} identify a nonlinear ``first drop of ink'' effect: a small amount of misleading information can disproportionately degrade reasoning. CUB evaluates context-utilization techniques across gold, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts \citep{rrag032}, while UDCG redefines retrieval evaluation around downstream utility rather than traditional relevance alone \citep{rrag058}.

Evidence-side defenses operate before or during context construction. They include retriever retraining, reranking, filtering, passage compression, and context ordering. Filtering can be document-level or sentence-level. FILCO-style sentence filtering removes irrelevant local content inside otherwise useful passages \citep{rrag044}; this is important because a retrieved document can contain both answer evidence and distracting details. Utility-aware retrieval metrics and rerankers attempt to optimize what helps the generator, not what merely matches the query \citep{rrag058}. Context ordering and long-context tuning address cases where the same evidence set has different effects depending on position \citep{rrag039}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: RAG introduces a conflict structure that does not exist in standard closed-book generation. The model has parametric memory, the retriever supplies external evidence, and multiple retrieved passages may disagree. When these sources conflict, models can exhibit two opposite failures: over-compliance with false retrieved evidence or stubborn reliance on stale parametric knowledge. Tug-of-War constructs and studies internal--external conflict in retrieval-augmented language models \citep{tugOfWar2024}. Adaptive Chameleon and related work show that LLMs can be highly receptive to coherent counter-evidence but resistant under other conflict conditions \citep{rrag046}. Real-document conflict studies show that behavior under conflict is not only a synthetic benchmark artifact \citep{rrag112}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Corpus poisoning attacks insert malicious passages into the retrieval database so that they are returned for target queries. Early work on poisoning retrieval corpora demonstrates that small numbers of adversarial passages can manipulate dense retrieval \citep{poisoningRetrievalCorpora2023}. PoisonedRAG extends this threat to end-to-end generation: retrieved malicious passages can cause the LLM to output attacker-chosen answers \citep{poisonedRAG2024}. BadRAG, UniC-RAG, and related methods explore different trigger structures, optimization objectives, and attack settings \citep{badRAG2024,rrag049,rrag057}. The important lesson is that retrieval augmentation can amplify small corpus changes into large generation effects.

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: Paper centrally addresses distracting passages in RAG and proposes a distraction-aware metric.

brief_actual_contribution: Introduces UDCG, a utility- and distraction-aware retrieval evaluation metric that aligns IR scoring with LLM-consumer behavior, showing stronger correlation with end-to-end RAG accuracy than nDCG/MAP/MRR.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Distraction is stronger than irrelevance. A passage is distracting when it has negative marginal utility: adding it changes the answer, confidence, attribution, or reasoning path in a harmful direction. This explains why more retrieval is not always better. In long-context settings, retrieving more passages can increase the chance that a hard negative appears before or near useful evidence. \citet{rrag039} study long-context RAG and show why ordering and hard negatives become central once the generator can consume many passages. \citet{rrag003} identify a nonlinear ``first drop of ink'' effect: a small amount of misleading information can disproportionately degrade reasoning. CUB evaluates context-utilization techniques across gold, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts \citep{rrag032}, while UDCG redefines retrieval evaluation around downstream utility rather than traditional relevance alone \citep{rrag058}.

Evidence-side defenses operate before or during context construction. They include retriever retraining, reranking, filtering, passage compression, and context ordering. Filtering can be document-level or sentence-level. FILCO-style sentence filtering removes irrelevant local content inside otherwise useful passages \citep{rrag044}; this is important because a retrieved document can contain both answer evidence and distracting details. Utility-aware retrieval metrics and rerankers attempt to optimize what helps the generator, not what merely matches the query \citep{rrag058}. Context ordering and long-context tuning address cases where the same evidence set has different effects depending on position \citep{rrag039}.

Robust RAG metrics should be diagnostic. For retrieval, recall and nDCG should be complemented by negative-utility metrics that penalize distracting evidence \citep{rrag058}. For generation, exact match should be complemented by faithfulness, citation support, and claim-level entailment. For attacks, attack success rate should be paired with stealth, retrieval rate, injected-document budget, and transferability. For calibration, expected calibration error should be paired with selective risk and coverage. For control, the unit of evaluation should be an action trace: retrieve, filter, verify, answer, abstain, or ask clarification. This makes it possible to distinguish a lucky correct answer from a robust decision process.

usage_audits.category_or_section: Noisy retrieval, distraction, and context compression

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: Trains models to be robust to noisy retrieved documents via various document selection and adversarial training strategies.

brief_actual_contribution: Empirically shows that as LLM capacity grows, complex robust RAG training (sophisticated document selection, adversarial losses like RAAT/IRM) yields diminishing returns over simple training (e.g., random documents), attributing this to stronger models' inherent calibration, generalization, and attention patterns.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Training-based approaches expose the generator to noise so that it learns to separate relevant from irrelevant context \citep{raat2024,rrag091}. This can improve robustness but also raises a scalability question: robust training may be less effective or less necessary as base LLMs become stronger, and adversarially generated noise can overfit to a particular retriever or generator. Training-free approaches, such as filtering and note-taking, are easier to add to existing systems but depend on reliable relevance or sufficiency signals. A recurring pattern is that no single pre-generation control is sufficient: retrieval filtering reduces easy noise, reranking handles ordering, compression improves context budget, and downstream calibration remains necessary for residual uncertainty.

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes SURE-RAG, an aggregation protocol that turns pair-level claim-evidence relation distributions into answer-level sufficiency labels (supported/refuted/insufficient) with a calibrated selective-answering score, evaluated on a controlled HotpotQA-RAG v3 benchmark with risk-coverage and ECE metrics.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: We group robust RAG evaluation into six families: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Noise robustness}: performance as irrelevant or misleading passages are injected, removed, reordered, or ranked higher. \item \textbf{Distraction sensitivity}: whether answer or confidence changes when distractors are added while gold evidence remains available. \item \textbf{Conflict sensitivity}: whether the system detects and resolves parametric--retrieved or retrieved--retrieved contradictions. \item \textbf{Adversarial robustness}: attack success rate, poisoned retrieval rate, trigger robustness, defense bypass rate, and recovery after filtering. \item \textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction}: selective risk, abstention precision/recall, expected calibration error, and clarification quality. \item \textbf{End-to-end action quality}: whether the system chooses the right policy among answer, retrieve, re-retrieve, filter, abstain, or ask. \end{enumerate} Benchmarking work such as RGB, RAGTruth, robustness-at-query-level analyses, poisoning benchmarks, and uncertainty benchmarks provides pieces of this landscape \citep{rgb2023,ragTruth2024,queryRobustness2025}. RGB is useful because it separates RAG abilities rather than reporting one score \citep{rgb2023}. RAGTruth contributes fine-grained hallucination annotations that support detection and attribution \citep{ragTruth2024}. Query-level robustness work shows that the query--retrieval interface is itself fragile \citep{queryRobustness2025}. PoisonArena-style benchmarks and LIAR-style attack evaluations stress adversarial settings rather than benign retrieval noise \citep{rrag023,rrag035}. URAG and uncertainty benchmarks evaluate whether systems know when their answers are reliable \citep{rrag001,rrag093}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Many faithful RAG methods implicitly assume that retrieved context should be trusted. Robust RAG cannot make this assumption. Retrieved context can be stale, poisoned, incomplete, or irrelevant; parametric knowledge can be outdated or hallucinated. The correct policy depends on source reliability. Source preference studies ask which sources win under conflict \citep{rrag132}; ``who's who'' style evaluations study behavior under practical entity-level conflicts \citep{rrag110}. These works suggest that future systems should represent not only claims but also provenance, timestamp, authority, and consistency. In a high-stakes setting, the most robust answer may not be a single synthesized fact; it may be a statement that exposes disagreement and explains why one source is more credible.

\paragraph{Knowledge conflict and contextual faithfulness.} \citep{rrag002,rrag008,rrag013,rrag017,rrag024,rrag029,faithfulRAG2025,rrag031,rrag036,rrag038,rrag040,rrag042,rrag045,rrag046,tugOfWar2024,rrag065,rrag069,rrag071}; \citep{rrag076,rrag077,rrag086,rrag089,rrag092,rrag100,rrag105,rrag110,rrag112,rrag118,rrag130,rrag132,rrag147,rrag150,rrag152,rrag163,rrag176,rrag187}; \citep{rrag202,rrag204,rrag207,rrag209,rrag216,rrag220,rrag222,rrag223,rrag227}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: RAG introduces a conflict structure that does not exist in standard closed-book generation. The model has parametric memory, the retriever supplies external evidence, and multiple retrieved passages may disagree. When these sources conflict, models can exhibit two opposite failures: over-compliance with false retrieved evidence or stubborn reliance on stale parametric knowledge. Tug-of-War constructs and studies internal--external conflict in retrieval-augmented language models \citep{tugOfWar2024}. Adaptive Chameleon and related work show that LLMs can be highly receptive to coherent counter-evidence but resistant under other conflict conditions \citep{rrag046}. Real-document conflict studies show that behavior under conflict is not only a synthetic benchmark artifact \citep{rrag112}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: RAG systems are often expected to cite sources, but citations do not guarantee faithfulness. A model can cite a passage that is topically related but does not support the generated claim, or cite the correct document while generating a claim from parametric memory. RAGTruth provides fine-grained hallucination annotations for RAG outputs \citep{ragTruth2024}. Related grounding methods train models to quote source spans or decompose external and parametric semantics, but these are not substitutes for claim-level citation verification \citep{rrag115,rrag206}. The key challenge is granularity. Document-level citation is too coarse when a passage contains multiple claims, qualifiers, or contradictions. Claim-level or sentence-level attribution is more informative but requires reliable entailment, alignment, and segmentation.

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes DIGA, a black-box genetic-algorithm corpus poisoning attack that exploits retrievers' token-order insensitivity and bias towards influential tokens to craft adversarial passages efficiently.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Backdoor-style attacks make the threat more persistent. TrojanRAG and Phantom show that triggers can activate malicious behavior through retrieved contexts without changing the generator weights \citep{trojanRAG2024,phantom2024}. Other attacks optimize token-level substitutions, influential tokens, or attention-steering patterns \citep{rrag050,rrag052,rrag120}. brief_actual_contribution: Introduces two knowledge poisoning attacks (targeted TKPA and universal UKPA) against GraphRAG that modify a tiny fraction of source text to distort the constructed knowledge graph and evade existing defenses.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Index-side design also changes robustness. Smaller chunks improve retrieval granularity but can remove context needed for factual interpretation. Larger chunks preserve context but increase the chance of including distracting material. Hybrid sparse--dense retrieval can reduce some embedding failures but may increase redundancy. Graph-based, multimodal, and agentic/process-level RAG add structure but introduce new poisoning surfaces, as shown by GraphRAG poisoning, graph poisoning, and reasoning-style poisoning work \citep{rrag051,rrag127,rrag175}. Thus, evidence-centric robustness should be studied as a corpus construction problem, not only as a retriever ranking problem.

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: we present the first traceback system in RAG, RAGForensics, which traces poisoned texts from the knowledge database
tracing poisoned texts in RAG poisoning attacks

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes RAGForensics, a post-hoc traceback system that identifies poisoned texts in a RAG knowledge database from user feedback on incorrect outputs, evaluated against PoisonedRAG and instruction injection attacks.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Defenses against adversarial corruption operate at multiple layers. Certified approaches such as RobustRAG isolate and aggregate outputs to provide guarantees under bounded retrieval corruption \citep{certifiedRAG2024}. Reranking defenses such as ProGRank use instability or probe-gradient signals to demote suspicious passages \citep{rrag004}. Attention-based filters detect abnormal attention patterns caused by poisoned evidence \citep{rrag015}. Clustering and conflict-resolution defenses such as TrustRAG and SeCon-RAG filter semantically inconsistent or suspicious evidence before generation \citep{rrag013,rrag017}. Traceback methods attempt to identify poisoned texts after an attack has occurred \citep{rrag128}.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Many faithful RAG methods implicitly assume that retrieved context should be trusted. Robust RAG cannot make this assumption. Retrieved context can be stale, poisoned, incomplete, or irrelevant; parametric knowledge can be outdated or hallucinated. The correct policy depends on source reliability. Source preference studies ask which sources win under conflict \citep{rrag132}; ``who's who'' style evaluations study behavior under practical entity-level conflicts \citep{rrag110}. These works suggest that future systems should represent not only claims but also provenance, timestamp, authority, and consistency. In a high-stakes setting, the most robust answer may not be a single synthesized fact; it may be a statement that exposes disagreement and explains why one source is more credible.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Evidence noise does not begin at retrieval scoring. Query formulation is itself a brittle interface. Query-level robustness work shows that minor changes in wording can substantially affect retrieval and downstream answers \citep{queryRobustness2025}. This suggests that robust RAG should include query normalization, query expansion, and query uncertainty estimation. In multi-turn settings, the query may be non-standalone or under-specified, making retrieval quality depend on dialogue state tracking \citep{rrag141}. The retriever may also inherit biases from chunking and indexing: relevant facts can be split across chunks, qualifiers can be separated from claims, and embeddings can overemphasize topical similarity over answer sufficiency.

The most basic control question is whether the available evidence is sufficient. RGB's negative rejection task and counterfactual robustness task show that RAG systems often answer when they should reject unsupported or false evidence \citep{rgb2023}. Sufficient Context reframes the problem: rather than asking whether the model can answer, ask whether the retrieved context contains enough information to answer \citep{sufficientContext2024}. Unanswerability benchmarks extend this idea to underspecified and unsupported queries \citep{rrag111,rrag141}.

Abstention should not be treated as a single fallback string. A RAG system can refuse, ask a clarifying question, retrieve more, answer partially with caveats, or expose conflicting evidence. Multi-turn unanswerability benchmarks show that robust systems must distinguish between genuinely unanswerable questions, underspecified questions requiring clarification, and answerable questions requiring retrieval \citep{rrag141}. The next step is interactive calibration: a system should not only know when it is uncertain but also choose the user-facing action that best reduces risk.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Index-side design also changes robustness. Smaller chunks improve retrieval granularity but can remove context needed for factual interpretation. Larger chunks preserve context but increase the chance of including distracting material. Hybrid sparse--dense retrieval can reduce some embedding failures but may increase redundancy. Graph-based, multimodal, and agentic/process-level RAG add structure but introduce new poisoning surfaces, as shown by GraphRAG poisoning, graph poisoning, and reasoning-style poisoning work \citep{rrag051,rrag127,rrag175}. contexts_supplied.paragraph: Recent benchmarks make this point more explicit. Magic Mushroom introduces fine-grained retrieval noise categories, including distracting and low-quality evidence \citep{rrag027}. URAG formulates uncertainty quantification in RAG and studies the effect of irrelevant and noisy retrieval on conformal prediction \citep{rrag001}. PRGB and other placeholder or perturbation-based benchmarks test whether models remain robust when retrieval context is systematically manipulated \citep{rrag183}. The trajectory of this literature is clear: robust RAG evaluation is moving from ``add random distractors'' to controlled stress tests that expose distinct failure mechanisms.

brief_actual_contribution: DSSP-RAG mitigates LLM hallucinations in RAG by combining unsupervised hallucination detection (sampling subspace stability), an Energy-Quotient-based external-knowledge noise filter, and a mixed-attention module that disentangles shared vs. private semantics between parametric and retrieved knowledge to resolve context-memory conflicts.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: RAG systems are often expected to cite sources, but citations do not guarantee faithfulness. A model can cite a passage that is topically related but does not support the generated claim, or cite the correct document while generating a claim from parametric memory. RAGTruth provides fine-grained hallucination annotations for RAG outputs \citep{ragTruth2024}. Related grounding methods train models to quote source spans or decompose external and parametric semantics, but these are not substitutes for claim-level citation verification \citep{rrag115,rrag206}. The key challenge is granularity. Document-level citation is too coarse when a passage contains multiple claims, qualifiers, or contradictions. Claim-level or sentence-level attribution is more informative but requires reliable entailment, alignment, and segmentation.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: \paragraph{Evidence reliability dimensions.} We use \emph{evidence reliability} as an umbrella concept with six dimensions. \textbf{Relevance} asks whether the evidence is about the query. \textbf{Sufficiency} asks whether it contains enough information to answer. \textbf{Faithfulness support} asks whether the final claim is entailed by the evidence rather than merely related. \textbf{Consistency} asks whether different evidence sources agree. \textbf{Provenance and freshness} ask where the evidence came from and whether it is up to date. \textbf{Integrity} asks whether the evidence has been manipulated. Existing work usually studies one or two of these dimensions at a time. For example, irrelevant-context robustness focuses on relevance and distraction \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, sufficient-context work focuses on answerability \citep{sufficientContext2024}, conflict work focuses on consistency \citep{tugOfWar2024,faithfulRAG2025}, and poisoning work focuses on integrity \citep{poisonedRAG2024,badRAG2024}. A central goal of this survey is to place these dimensions in one framework.

The most basic control question is whether the available evidence is sufficient. RGB's negative rejection task and counterfactual robustness task show that RAG systems often answer when they should reject unsupported or false evidence \citep{rgb2023}. Sufficient Context reframes the problem: rather than asking whether the model can answer, ask whether the retrieved context contains enough information to answer \citep{sufficientContext2024}. Unanswerability benchmarks extend this idea to underspecified and unsupported queries \citep{rrag111,rrag141}.

This intervention map helps explain why papers sometimes appear to solve the same problem while actually operating at different layers. For example, irrelevant-context filtering \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, Chain-of-Note \citep{chainOfNote2023}, and Sufficient Context \citep{sufficientContext2024} all address unreliable evidence, but the first filters evidence, the second changes generator reasoning, and the third changes answer policy. Similarly, PoisonedRAG-style attacks \citep{poisonedRAG2024} target the corpus-to-generation path, while AIP attacks prompt templates \citep{aip2025}. A comprehensive survey must therefore compare methods by intervention point, not only by reported task accuracy.

title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: explores knowledge conflicts between internal memory and external sources, and between truthful, irrelevant and misleading evidence
Tug-of-War constructs internal-external knowledge conflicts in RALMs and analyzes both over-compliance and stubborn parametric reliance (Dunning-Kruger effect)
Focus on exploring and resolving knowledge conflicts in RALMs.

brief_actual_contribution: Proposes an evaluation framework for knowledge conflicts in RALMs (internal vs. external and among external evidence), reveals Dunning-Kruger-like and confirmation bias behaviors, and introduces Conflict-Disentangle Contrastive Decoding (CD2) to calibrate model confidence.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: \paragraph{Evidence reliability dimensions.} We use \emph{evidence reliability} as an umbrella concept with six dimensions. \textbf{Relevance} asks whether the evidence is about the query. \textbf{Sufficiency} asks whether it contains enough information to answer. \textbf{Faithfulness support} asks whether the final claim is entailed by the evidence rather than merely related. \textbf{Consistency} asks whether different evidence sources agree. \textbf{Provenance and freshness} ask where the evidence came from and whether it is up to date. \textbf{Integrity} asks whether the evidence has been manipulated. Existing work usually studies one or two of these dimensions at a time. For example, irrelevant-context robustness focuses on relevance and distraction \citep{irrelevantContext2023}, sufficient-context work focuses on answerability \citep{sufficientContext2024}, conflict work focuses on consistency \citep{tugOfWar2024,faithfulRAG2025}, and poisoning work focuses on integrity \citep{poisonedRAG2024,badRAG2024}. A central goal of this survey is to place these dimensions in one framework.

RAG introduces a conflict structure that does not exist in standard closed-book generation. The model has parametric memory, the retriever supplies external evidence, and multiple retrieved passages may disagree. When these sources conflict, models can exhibit two opposite failures: over-compliance with false retrieved evidence or stubborn reliance on stale parametric knowledge. Tug-of-War constructs and studies internal--external conflict in retrieval-augmented language models \citep{tugOfWar2024}. Adaptive Chameleon and related work show that LLMs can be highly receptive to coherent counter-evidence but resistant under other conflict conditions \citep{rrag046}. Real-document conflict studies show that behavior under conflict is not only a synthetic benchmark artifact \citep{rrag112}.

\paragraph{Knowledge conflict and contextual faithfulness.} \citep{rrag002,rrag008,rrag013,rrag017,rrag024,rrag029,faithfulRAG2025,rrag031,rrag036,rrag038,rrag040,rrag042,rrag045,rrag046,tugOfWar2024,rrag065,rrag069,rrag071}; \citep{rrag076,rrag077,rrag086,rrag089,rrag092,rrag100,rrag105,rrag110,rrag112,rrag118,rrag130,rrag132,rrag147,rrag150,rrag152,rrag163,rrag176,rrag187}; \citep{rrag202,rrag204,rrag207,rrag209,rrag216,rrag220,rrag222,rrag223,rrag227}.

title: Tug-of-War Between Knowledge: Exploring and Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: span uncertainty enhances model calibration, improving robustness and mitigating semantic inconsistencies introduced by random chunking
AUROC used to evaluate uncertainty calibration of LLMs; their span uncertainty shows better calibration than other methods

usage_audits.problem_if_any: The paper uses span-level uncertainty primarily to train the retrieval model (construct positive/negative pairs via SNR-based similarity), not directly to improve robustness under distribution shift in generation. The claim 'improve retrieval training and robustness under distribution shift' is accurate to the paper.
usage_audits.suggested_revision: Current usage is acceptable; could be more precisely framed as 'span-level uncertainty for unsupervised retrieval training, with calibration benefits under distribution shift.'

brief_actual_contribution: Introduces UncertaintyRAG, which uses SNR-based span-level uncertainty from an LLM to score chunk-pair similarity, enabling unsupervised training of a lightweight retrieval model for long-context RAG that generalizes under distribution shift.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Calibration asks whether confidence matches correctness. In RAG, confidence depends on both model uncertainty and evidence uncertainty. CalibRAG optimizes for calibrated decision-making \citep{calibRAG2025}; UncertaintyRAG uses span-level uncertainty to improve retrieval training and robustness under distribution shift \citep{uncertaintyRAG2024}; noise-aware verbal confidence calibration targets overconfidence under irrelevant or counterfactual retrieval \citep{rrag007}. SABER-style trust-or-abstain approaches estimate whether parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge paths are reliable, then map them to trust and abstention decisions \citep{rrag002}.

title: UncertaintyRAG: Span-Level Uncertainty Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence.quote_or_precise_paraphrase: LLMs are trained to generate a special token, <RET>, when they do not know the answer to a question.

brief_actual_contribution: Introduces ADAPT-LLM, which fine-tunes an LLM to emit a special <RET> token to trigger external retrieval only when its parametric memory is insufficient, evaluated on PopQA.

contexts_supplied.paragraph: Always retrieving is inefficient and can be harmful; never retrieving leaves the model dependent on stale parametric knowledge. Adaptive retrieval methods learn or infer when external evidence is needed. Self-RAG trains models to retrieve, generate, and critique with reflection tokens \citep{selfRAG2023}. Adapt-LLM-style methods use explicit retrieval tokens to signal when retrieval is needed \citep{whenToRetrieve2024}. CtrlA uses representation-level honesty and confidence directions to guide retrieval timing \citep{ctrla2025}. Corrective RAG uses a retrieval evaluator to trigger additional retrieval or web search when the initial evidence is weak \citep{crag2024}.

title: When to Retrieve: Teaching LLMs to Utilize Information Retrieval Effectively
